Chapter 9: Reflections on Justice, Privilege, and the Need for Reform.
Looking back, you can't help but wonder—how fair is the system, really? Prison has a way of shining a harsh light on the cracks in our justice system, and it’s usually the people with the least who feel those cracks the most.
So many women behind those walls come from lives shaped by poverty, trauma, and far too few opportunities. A lot of the time, the choices that land them in prison aren’t just about breaking the law—they’re about surviving, about battling addiction, or just trying to make it through another day.
But instead of helping folks address what’s really going on underneath, the system just punishes—and then expects everything to get better on its own.
And then there’s privilege. You really start to notice how much it matters—how someone’s access to money, education, or even just knowing the right people can shape their entire experience.
Two people might be charged with the same thing, but their outcomes? Completely different. If you can afford a good lawyer, the odds are in your favor. Race, class, gender—they all play a part, sometimes in ways you barely notice, but they add up.
I remember one woman who realized just how much her own background protected her. She saw others—women without the same safety nets—facing longer sentences, tougher conditions, and almost no chance at an early release. That sense of injustice? It’s impossible to ignore.
Here’s the truth: we can’t keep pretending that small tweaks and new policies are enough. Real reform means rethinking how we see crime, punishment, and what it actually means to give someone a second chance. Programs that focus on rehabilitation, education, and mental health—they aren’t just nice extras, they’re essential if we want things to change.
But it takes more than that. It takes seeing people as more than their worst mistakes. When you really look at it, justice shouldn’t just be about punishment—it should be about healing. About helping people rebuild, restore, and find a way back to their communities.
